conflicts.about: Field validation on arrival details and transit countries: Design Release 2.1 validates softly (only means of transport raises an error), while the real service refuses bad dates, unknown ports and codes, over-long text, repeated or unknown countries and more than 12 countries.

positions.says: A real constraint the prototype cannot express, validation among them, overrides the prototype default.
No error is shown for a missing, badly formed or out-of-range arrival date; it only affects completeness.
No error is shown for a missing or unrecognised port of entry.
Transport identification has no format or length check.
Transport document reference has no format or length check.
The server does not check that a transit country is on the list or not repeated.
When the means of transport error shows, everything else entered is still saved.
An arrival date that is not a real date is refused with 'Enter a real arrival date'.
A port not in the list is refused with 'Select a valid option'.
Transport identification over 58 characters is refused.
Adding a country already in the list is refused by name.
At most 12 transit countries can be added.
When the arrival date is out of window nothing on the page is saved.

conflicts.outcome: The ruling ranks first and names validation as a real constraint the prototype cannot express, so the real service keeps every server-side field check and its message: the real-date and window checks on the arrival date, the stale-date and stale-port flags, the in-list checks on port and means of transport, the 58-character limits, and the transit checks (nothing chosen, not on the list, already added, the 12-country cap, stale saved countries). A page with any error saves nothing and shows the entries back. Where Design Release 2.1 does validate (means of transport required on Save and continue) it is adopted. The prototype's soft-validation claims are set aside.

conflicts.about: What the pages submit and store: Design Release 2.1 posts display text (the port as 'name - code', transit countries as a JSON list of names, means of transport as 'Air'), while the real service submits and stores reference codes.

positions.says: The prototype never decides form field names or data-model shape, and c-047 is kept for a real constraint.
A real constraint the prototype cannot express, persistence and cross-service behaviour among them, overrides the prototype default.
The port of entry is posted as the display string 'name - code', not a separate code.
The arrival form posts the means of transport as 'Air' and the port as its display string.
Transit countries are submitted as a JSON list in one hidden field.
Means of transport values are normalised to and stored as Air, Rail, Road and Sea.
Chosen transit countries are held in a hidden field as a JSON array of names.
The transit form posts transitCountries as a URL-encoded JSON array.
Transit countries are submitted as one hidden JSON array of country names.
Transit countries are submitted as one hidden JSON list built client-side.
Each port option submits the port code.
The transited countries answer is saved as a list of country codes.
Each port carries MDM's port code.

conflicts.outcome: The rulings rank first: the stored answer is read by the backend and other services, a persistence and cross-service constraint the prototype cannot express, and Sam's 9 October ruling keeps c-047 and says the prototype never decides form field names or data shape. The real service keeps submitting and storing the port code, the means-of-transport code (AIRPLANE, RAILWAY, ROAD_VEHICLE, VESSEL) and transit country codes. What the user sees still follows Design Release 2.1 (labels, option text), so only the submitted and stored form is set aside.

conflicts.about: The content and order of the port of entry and transit country lists: Design Release 2.1 offers its own 205 ports (airports by traffic, then seaports A to Z, no rail) and 41 countries; DR1's judgement deferred list content to the MDM integration and blocked the list rows; Sam's 9 October ruling builds every list now from what MDM serves, ordered by port type.

positions.says: Every reference list is built now against reference-data as it is, and its content is what MDM serves.
Where a list's content differs from Design Release 2.1, that is MDM's content to change, never a reason to block a row or edit a list in code.
The block is taken off the requirements behind c-048.
Within each port group (airports, seaports, rail) ports are sorted A to Z by name ignoring letter case.
The transit country search offers the GBNAG_SPS_EX countries plus their subdivisions.
A parity finding whose fix is the content of a master reference-data list is deferred rather than built, because MDM replaces it.
The country-list and port-list increments are blocked on MDM grounds and need a fresh ruling.
The port of entry list holds 205 entries: 28 airports then 177 seaports.
The airports are listed busiest first, London Heathrow to Dundee, not A to Z.
The rendered port list starts London Heathrow, London Gatwick, Manchester, then seaports from Aberdeen.
The transit country search offers the EU member states, outermost territories and Crown Dependencies.
The transit country list offers 41 options: EU states, outermost regions and Crown Dependencies.
Ports are read from MDM's border control post points-of-entry list.
Ports are returned sorted by name.
The transit country list is the countries service's origin-country list.

conflicts.outcome: Sam's 9 October ruling ranks first. No list waits on MDM: the port list and the transit country list are built now against reference-data as it is, and their content is what MDM serves (real MDM in CDP test, the tidied stub locally and in CDP dev). Design Release 2.1's 205 ports and 41 countries are not built, and no list is edited in code; the duplicate and misspelt ports go to the MDM team as a content report. The port list is ordered airports, seaports, then rail, each group A to Z ignoring case, from MDM's traffic field. The transit search offers the GBNAG_SPS_EX countries plus their subdivisions labelled '<territory> (<parent>)'. DR1's judgement (document-dr1-parity-notes-p1-038) still stands for who owns list content, so it is not overruled; its block on the list rows is withdrawn.

conflicts.about: Which arrival date Design Release 2.1 collects: its question page asks for the arrival date at the port of entry, but its review page labels the same answer 'Arrival date at destination'.

positions.says: The arrival details page labels the field 'Arrival date at port of entry'.
The review labels the arrival date 'Arrival date at destination'.
DR1 contradicted itself the same way between its question page and its review page and dashboard cards.
Whether the date is arrival at the port of entry or at the destination is undecided, and nothing changes until it is ruled.
The real frontend labels the question, the check-answers row and the validation message 'Arrival date at port of entry'.
Nothing other than a DR1 judgement on the same difference or a real constraint the prototype cannot express overrides the prototype.
DR1 deferred the arrival date label finding (inc-145) with the disputed band, to be revisited as a group.

conflicts.outcome: The arrival date is the expected arrival at the port of entry, as Design Release 2.1's arrival details page asks for it, hints it and stores it (arrivalDateAtPort). The question page, the review row and the out-of-window error message all read 'Arrival date at port of entry'; the prototype's review label 'Arrival date at destination' contradicts the data its own question collects and is not copied. The real service already does this, so nothing changes.

conflicts.about: The worked example in the arrival date hint: Design Release 2.1 uses a fixed '27/3/2026', while the real service shows today's date so the example is always a date the window accepts.

positions.says: A real constraint the prototype cannot express, validation among them, overrides the prototype default.
The hint is 'The expected date of arrival at the port of entry. For example, 27/3/2026'.
The rendered hint ends 'For example, 27/3/2026'.
The spec asserts the hint with the fixed example 27/3/2026.
The example is today's date in Europe/London.
The worked example is always a date the page accepts.

conflicts.outcome: The ruling ranks first. The real service keeps its arrival-date window (conflict on validation), and a fixed 27/3/2026 already falls outside that window, so a user who copied the example would be refused. The validation the prototype cannot express overrides its fixed example: the hint keeps its Design Release 2.1 wording with today's date as the example.

conflicts.about: Where the arrival details page lives: Design Release 2.1 serves it at 'arrival-details', the real service at 'port-of-entry'.

positions.says: req-271 and inc-025 (arrival details moving to 'arrival-details') are dropped as out of scope.
No increment changes an existing real URL path to match the prototype.
The arrival details page is served at /arrival-details.
The arrival details form posts to /arrival-details.
The page is served at the slug 'port-of-entry'.
The page object opens the page at 'port-of-entry'.
The k6 script requests the page at 'port-of-entry'.

conflicts.outcome: Sam's 9 October ruling ranks first: the prototype never decides URL paths, so the page stays at 'port-of-entry' and req-271 is out of scope. Everything the user sees on the page still follows Design Release 2.1. The form's post target (prototype-dr2-1-source-p6-011) is not overruled, because the same claim still backs the form turning off browser validation (req-334); only its path is set aside.

conflicts.about: How matches are shown in the port search results: Design Release 2.1 bolds the matched part of each option, while the real accessible-autocomplete shows plain options.

positions.says: inc-027 does not copy bold matches (req-299).
The autocomplete behaves as the real frontend configures it, including how matches are shown.
Bold matches are not copied into plants' place of landing search.
The port search shows options as 'name - code' and highlights what matches.
Today's accessible-autocomplete menu shows each option as plain text.

conflicts.outcome: The 9 October afternoon ruling ranks first: how matches are shown follows the accessible-autocomplete as the real frontend configures it, so bold matches are not built in animals or plants and req-299 is out of scope. The prototype claim is not overruled, because it still backs the 'name - code' labels (req-295) and the name-and-code filtering (req-297); only its bold highlighting is set aside.

conflicts.about: Accessibility and no-JavaScript shortfalls on Design Release 2.1's arrival and transit pages: its error page title has no 'Error: ' prefix, and its transit Remove links are href='#' links that work only with JavaScript and name no country, while the real service prefixes the title and uses Remove buttons that submit the form with the country's name in visually hidden text.

positions.says: Every page works fully without JavaScript; CSS and JavaScript may only enhance a page that already works.
Without JavaScript the transit countries page keeps today's native select, the 'Add country' button and the Remove buttons that submit the form.
GDS components are the toolbox; the prototype's JavaScript behaviour is not to be blindly copied.
With a validation error the arrival details page title gains no 'Error: ' prefix.
The transit 'Remove' links have href='#' and work only with JavaScript.
Each transit 'Remove' link reads only 'Remove', with no visually hidden country name.
Today the arrival details title is prefixed with 'Error: ' when the page shows an error.
Today each transit Remove control carries the country's name in visually hidden text.

conflicts.outcome: The 9 October afternoon ruling ranks first: every page works without JavaScript and the GOV.UK toolbox is used, so the real service keeps the 'Error: ' title prefix on arrival details and transit countries, the Remove buttons that submit the form, and the visually hidden country name on each Remove (req-350, req-351, req-352). Nothing changes; the prototype's unprefixed title and JavaScript-only, unnamed Remove links are not copied. This applies c-006's accessibility outcome to the two claims that conflict did not list.
